content:
Epic Games has submitted a response to Apple's request for the court to order both parties into settlement negotiations. Details are as follows.

Epic believes court-ordered settlement negotiations would not be beneficial

Last Thursday, Apple submitted a proposed commission structure for in-app purchases made within the United States through channels outside the App Store system.

Under Apple's proposed structure, the company would charge a commission of up to 15% on purchases completed through alternative payment systems.

On the same day, Apple filed another motion requesting Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers to order both parties to attend a settlement conference.

In its motion, Apple stated that "discussing potential settlement options in a confidential, non-adversarial environment would increase the chances of reaching a pragmatic resolution, thereby avoiding lengthy remand proceedings."

Epic has now responded to Apple's motion, stating that while the company "has been and remains willing to consider any direct outreach from Apple, provided the other side presents a serious settlement proposal that introduces competition and benefits all developers," it "does not believe that referring the case to a settlement conference at this time would effectively increase the chances of reaching such a settlement."

Epic added in its response that "if the Court orders the case referred to a settlement conference, Epic will participate in good faith."

It now falls to Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers to decide whether to refer the case to a settlement conference; Apple has requested that the conference be conducted under the supervision of Magistrate Judge Joseph C. Spero.

You can read Epic's full response below:

9to5Mac Opinion

Apple has repeatedly attempted to narrow the scope of the injunction issued by Judge Gonzalez Rogers concerning purchases made through channels outside the App Store. Apple particularly argued that, since Epic's lawsuit is not a class action, the injunction should not apply broadly to other developers.

For example, Apple argued in one of its appeals that developers seeking similar relief should file their own lawsuits rather than benefit from the injunction in Epic's case. The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals rejected Apple's arguments to narrow the injunction's scope, ruling that limiting the injunction to apply only to Epic and its affiliates would not provide Epic with the complete relief it sought.

The reasoning behind this ruling is also consistent with the public position Epic has held for most of the case—that its fight transcends its own commercial interests and aims to benefit developers more broadly.

In its motion requesting the case be referred to (confidential) settlement negotiations, Apple did not indicate what proposal it might put forward. However, anyone following this case closely would likely agree that Apple would probably seek a deal particularly attractive to Epic while limiting any concessions to Epic alone.

In fact, Epic's response preempts this idea, stating that Apple's "serious settlement proposal" must "benefit all developers," and in the closing of its response, hints that Apple's efforts may be too little, too late.

If you were Apple, what proposal would you put to Epic Games? Let us know in the comments.
